 FINANCIAL FOCUS®: Making the most of Medicare open enrollment 
 Submitted by Jess Williams
Edward Jones

 4 hrs ago

 When you turn 65, Medicare becomes a vital part of your health care coverage. But Medicare isn't a "set it and forget it" program. In fact, you have the opportunity to review and adjust your coverage every year.
 The annual Medicare Open Enrollment period, which runs from Oct. 15 through Dec. 7 each year, is your chance to take a fresh look at your health care needs and ensure your Medicare plan still fits your life. Changes made during this period generally take effect Jan. 1 of the following year.
 Just as your health can change from year to year, Medicare plans can change too. Insurance companies may adjust their coverage and costs or even discontinue certain plans. If you take no action during open enrollment, you'll generally remain in your current plan if it's still available. That's why it's worth reviewing your options each year. You may find coverage that better meets your needs or lowers your costs.
 You have several options when it comes to Medicare coverage:
 Original Medicare (Parts A and B) covers hospital stays and medical services such as doctor visits. Part A typically comes with no monthly premium if you've worked for at least 10 years. Part B requires a monthly premium, with higher-income beneficiaries paying additional amounts based on income. Part B also includes an annual deductible and cost-sharing requirements, with Medicare typically announcing updated amounts for the coming year in November.
 Medicare Advantage (Part C) offers an all-in-one alternative to Original Medicare through private insurance companies. Many plans bundle Part A, Part B and usually Part D while including additional benefits like vision and dental coverage.
 Medicare Part D provides standalone prescription drug coverage for those who stay with Original Medicare. In 2027, Part D plans include a $2,400 annual cap on out-of-pocket spending for covered prescription medications, although covered drugs vary by plan.
 Medicare Supplement (Medigap) policies help cover certain out-of-pocket costs that Original Medicare doesn't pay.
 When evaluating Medicare plans, consider these factors:
 Out-of-pocket costs , including premiums, deductibles, copayments and other expenses not covered by Medicare.
 Prescription drug coverage. Although Part D plans include a $2,400 cap on out-of-pocket spending for covered drugs in 2027, the medications covered by each plan can vary. Make sure your prescriptions are included.
 Provider access. Make sure your doctors and hospitals are covered by the plan.
 Your anticipated health care needs. If you expect ongoing treatment, specialist care or planned procedures, make sure your plan provides appropriate coverage.
 Travel considerations. Frequent travelers may want supplemental coverage for emergencies outside the U.S.
 Even if you're satisfied with your current coverage, don't assume next year's plan will look exactly the same. Costs, provider networks and the medications covered by a plan can change from year to year, making a quick annual review worthwhile.
 Don't let your Medicare plan run on autopilot. Take advantage of the annual open enrollment period between Oct. 15 and Dec. 7 to help ensure your coverage continues to meet your needs in the year ahead.
